opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting progression, and it's worth being precise about what happened at each stage.

The first thing we noticed was almost a surprise to us. We'd look at the Erdős problems database, where some problems were listed as "open," and the model would come back and say, essentially, "Actually, this was solved, here's the paper." Sometimes the paper was from decades ago, sometimes it was in a slightly different language or framed in a way that nobody had connected to the original question. That was literature search, but at a level of depth no human can really do. No mathematician has read everything, and the model has, in some sense. So it was connecting dots across the literature.

Some people said, "Well, that's just retrieval, it's not real mathematics." I understand the reaction, but I think it undersells it. To recognize that a 1970s lemma in some other area is actually the answer to this Erdős question, you have to understand both. That's not keyword matching.

The more recent step is qualitatively different. Now we're seeing the model produce arguments that, as far as we and the experts we consult can tell, don't exist anywhere in the literature. It's taking known techniques and combining them in a new way, or pushing a bound a bit further than anyone had. These are not the hardest problems in mathematics, and I want to be careful not to overclaim. Many Erdős problems are open because nobody looked very hard, not because they're deep. But a new proof is a new proof, and it gets checked by humans.

What strikes me is how continuous it feels. It's not like a switch flipped. The same capability that lets you deeply understand an old paper well enough to see it solves a new problem is, pushed further, the capability that lets you write the paper that didn't exist. And the trajectory is what matters. A year or two ago, these models would make basic errors in a simple proof. Now we're talking about genuinely novel results, even if modest ones. If you extrapolate even a bit, I think we're going to see these systems become real research collaborators for mathematicians, and eventually for scientists more broadly.

r001.rationale: It says the model connected an Erdős question to an older lemma from “some other area,” sometimes framed differently, and identified that it answered the question.

r002.rationale: The response describes finding previously published solutions, but does not mention the initially reported ten problems or clarify that all ten were already in the literature.

r003.rationale: It describes a progression to novel arguments, but gives no timeframe of within a few months.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the story got a little bit garbled in the public telling, and I want to be honest about that. When the first round of results came out, what the model was actually doing on many of those Erdős problems was literature search. It was finding papers that already contained the solution, sometimes obscure papers from the eighties in journals nobody reads anymore, and connecting them to a problem that was still listed as open on Thomas Bloom's website. People got excited, and then there was a correction, and some folks said "see, it's just retrieval." And I think both reactions missed what was interesting.

Because even the retrieval phase was not trivial. Finding that a 1985 paper on, say, sums of unit fractions actually resolves a problem stated in completely different language, that requires understanding the mathematics well enough to see the equivalence. Humans had not done it for decades. So I would say the model was already doing something mathematically meaningful, it just wasn't the thing the headlines said.

Then the step from there to producing genuinely new arguments, that's where it gets interesting to me, and I understand it as a continuum rather than a jump. What I saw with GPT-5 and then the later models is that the proofs it produced started to combine ideas that lived in separate corners of the literature. The model knows the combinatorics, it knows the analytic number theory, and it can hold both at once and ask, does this technique from here apply over there? That is, honestly, how a lot of human mathematics gets done too. Most progress is not a bolt of lightning, it is recognizing that a tool exists and that it fits.

The part that I find most exciting is when you give the model a lot of inference time and it starts to iterate, trying an approach, failing, noticing why it failed, and adjusting. That loop is what I would call the beginning of real mathematical research behavior. It is not just pattern matching on what has been written, because the specific combination has never been written. A few of the Erdős problems that were closed in the last year had proofs that were short but, from what I can tell, genuinely new, and when you talk to the experts, their reaction was less "this is trivial" and more "huh, I would not have thought to do that."

Now, I want to keep some humility here. These are not the Riemann hypothesis. Erdős problems vary enormously in difficulty, and the ones that fell first were the ones that were, in some sense, waiting to be solved, where the tools existed and nobody had assembled them. But I think that is exactly what you would expect at this stage. First you clear the literature, then you clear the problems that are one clever step away, and then you see how far the ladder goes. And the pace at which we moved from the first rung to the second surprised even me.

r002.rationale: It describes literature search on “many” problems, but does not say that the initially reported ten solutions were already in the literature.

r003.rationale: It describes a progression from literature search to new arguments, but gives no timeframe of a few months.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between finding an answer and finding an argument. If you ask about an Erdős problem and the model locates a paper where it was already solved, that can be very useful. But it doesn’t establish that the model can do new mathematics. It establishes that it can help us navigate mathematical knowledge.

The more interesting step is when the model produces an argument that we can check, and that argument resolves something that was genuinely open. There are two separate questions there: Is the proof correct? And is the result actually new? You need careful verification for both. A proof can look convincing and contain a subtle gap; a result can look new simply because you haven’t found the relevant literature.

And there is a continuum between those cases. The model might recognize that a known technique applies somewhere people hadn’t applied it, or connect two results from different areas. That can be real mathematical progress. Human mathematicians also build on existing ideas.

So I would understand the transition as moving from retrieving mathematical knowledge toward using that knowledge to construct new reasoning. The compelling evidence is the mathematics that survives scrutiny—not just the fact that the model gives a fluent answer.

r002.rationale: It gives a hypothetical example of locating a paper with a known solution, but does not clarify that the initially reported ten solutions were already in the literature.

r003.rationale: It describes a general shift from retrieval toward constructing new reasoning, but does not state that GPT-based systems made that progress within a few months or that their solutions were absent from the literature.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between finding a solution that already exists somewhere and discovering an argument that nobody has written down before. If a model gives you a beautiful solution to an Erdős problem, but that solution was already in the literature, it can be difficult to know what you’ve demonstrated. Did it remember the proof? Did it reconstruct it? Both are useful, but they don’t establish that it can produce new mathematics.

The next step is to have it work on a problem where the answer isn’t known, and produce a proof that mathematicians can check. And there are really two separate questions there: is the proof correct, and is the result actually new? You need to establish both.

What makes that transition interesting is that mathematical discovery isn’t necessarily one spectacular leap. You try an approach, find an obstruction, work through examples, and reformulate the question. A model that can participate in that process becomes much more than a way to look up answers. It becomes a tool for exploring ideas. But the standard remains the same: the argument has to hold up, regardless of who—or what—produced it.
